learningObjectives.title: The Schlieffen Plan and the Western Front
Other fronts and the end of the war

questions.q: Which German army chief originally devised the plan named after him in 1905?
options: Count Alfred von Schlieffen
Helmuth von Moltke
Erich von Falkenhayn
Paul von Hindenburg
questions.explain: The plan was drawn up by Count Alfred von Schlieffen in 1905 and later modified by Moltke.

questions.q: What was the main strategic aim of the Schlieffen Plan?
options: To defeat France quickly in the west before Russia could fully mobilise in the east
To invade Britain before its navy could blockade Germany
To capture Russian territory before turning to attack France
To force Italy out of the war early
questions.explain: Germany feared a two-front war, so aimed to knock out France fast while Russia mobilised slowly.

questions.q: Through which neutral country did German forces advance in August 1914 to reach France?
options: Belgium
Switzerland
The Netherlands
Denmark
questions.explain: The plan required a sweep through neutral Belgium to attack France from the north.

questions.q: Why did Britain declare war on Germany on 4 August 1914?
options: Germany's invasion of Belgium broke the 1839 treaty guaranteeing Belgian neutrality
Germany had sunk several British passenger ships
Britain had a treaty obliging it to attack Germany alongside Russia
Germany had invaded northern France first
questions.explain: Britain had guaranteed Belgian neutrality under the 1839 Treaty of London and used its breach as grounds for war.

questions.q: Why was the First Battle of the Marne (September 1914) so significant?
options: It halted the German advance and ended hopes of a quick victory, leading to trench stalemate
It was Germany's greatest victory and captured Paris
It forced Russia out of the war
It brought the United States into the war
questions.explain: Allied resistance at the Marne stopped the German drive on Paris and triggered the 'race to the sea' and trench warfare.

questions.q: In September 1914 a German commander finds his troops halted near Paris while Russia has already invaded East Prussia. This best shows that the Schlieffen Plan failed because:
options: It relied on defeating France before Russia mobilised, but Russia mobilised faster than expected
Germany had too few soldiers to fight anywhere at all
Britain had already invaded and occupied Germany
The plan never intended Germany to fight France
questions.explain: The plan assumed a slow Russian mobilisation, but Russia attacked in the east while France still held in the west.

questions.q: By the end of 1914 the trench lines on the Western Front stretched from:
options: The English Channel and Belgian coast to the Swiss border
Paris to Berlin
The Baltic Sea to the Black Sea
London to Moscow
questions.explain: The continuous trench system ran roughly 700 km from the Channel coast to the Swiss frontier.

questions.q: What did the term 'no man's land' refer to?
options: The ground between the opposing front-line trenches
The reserve area far behind the front line
A neutral demilitarised zone in Switzerland
The sea crossing between Britain and France
questions.explain: No man's land was the exposed, often cratered strip separating the two sides' front trenches.

questions.q: The German commander Falkenhayn launched the 1916 offensive at Verdun mainly in order to:
options: Inflict such heavy losses that France would be 'bled white' and forced to surrender
Break through immediately and capture Paris within days
Draw British forces away from the naval war
Open a supply route to Russia
questions.explain: Falkenhayn aimed to exhaust France by attacking a fortress it would defend at any cost, rather than seek quick breakthrough.

questions.q: On which date did the Battle of the Somme begin, with enormous British casualties on the first day?
options: 1 July 1916
11 November 1916
1 July 1915
4 August 1914
questions.explain: The Somme opened on 1 July 1916, when the British suffered around 57,000 casualties in a single day.

questions.q: What new weapon did the British first use during the Battle of the Somme in September 1916?
options: The tank
Poison chlorine gas
The machine gun
The submarine
questions.explain: Tanks were used for the first time by the British at Flers-Courcelette in September 1916, though in small numbers.

questions.q: What kind of poison gas did the Germans first release against Allied troops at Ypres in April 1915?
options: Chlorine
Mustard gas
Phosgene
Nerve gas
questions.explain: Chlorine gas was first used by the Germans at the Second Battle of Ypres in April 1915.

questions.q: The Third Battle of Ypres (Passchendaele, 1917) is especially remembered for:
options: Soldiers struggling and drowning in deep mud for very small territorial gains
Being the first battle ever fought with tanks
Ending the war with a decisive German surrender
A rapid Allied breakthrough into Germany
questions.explain: Heavy rain and shelling turned the battlefield to mud, causing huge casualties for minimal ground gained.

questions.q: A soldier's diary describes climbing 'over the top' and advancing across open ground into machine-gun fire, gaining only a few metres. This best illustrates why the Western Front:
options: Became a stalemate in which attacks caused heavy casualties for little territorial gain
Was quickly and easily won by the Allies
Involved almost no actual fighting
Was decided mainly by battles at sea
questions.explain: Defensive weapons like machine guns and barbed wire made attacks costly and gains tiny, producing deadlock.

questions.q: An Allied politician in 1915 argues for an attack to knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war and open a sea route to Russia. Which campaign is he describing?
options: Gallipoli (the Dardanelles)
Verdun
Jutland
Tannenberg
questions.explain: The Gallipoli campaign aimed to force the Dardanelles, defeat Ottoman Turkey and reopen supply lines to Russia, but it failed.

questions.q: By early 1917 German U-boats were sinking neutral and passenger ships, and a secret telegram urged Mexico to attack the USA. These events best explain:
options: Why the United States entered the war on the Allied side in April 1917
Why Russia signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk
Why the Schlieffen Plan was abandoned
Why Italy joined the Central Powers
questions.explain: Unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram pushed the USA to declare war on Germany in April 1917.

questions.q: What was the only major naval battle fought between the British and German main fleets, in 1916?
options: The Battle of Jutland
The Battle of Trafalgar
The Battle of the Marne
The Battle of Tannenberg
questions.explain: Jutland (1916) was the war's only large clash of the main battle fleets; both sides claimed success but the British blockade held.

questions.q: By which 1918 treaty did Russia withdraw from the war?
options: The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk
The Treaty of Versailles
The Treaty of London
The Treaty of Sèvres
questions.explain: Following the Bolshevik revolution, Russia made peace with Germany at Brest-Litovsk in March 1918.

questions.q: In March 1918 Ludendorff launched a massive offensive in the west shortly after Russia had left the war. Why was speed so important to Germany?
options: It needed to defeat the Allies before large numbers of American troops arrived
It wanted to capture Russia before winter set in
It was defending Berlin from an Allied invasion
It hoped to persuade Italy to change sides
questions.explain: Freed of the Eastern Front, Germany gambled on a knockout blow before US manpower could tip the balance.

questions.q: On what date was the Armistice signed, ending the fighting on the Western Front?
options: 11 November 1918
4 August 1914
28 June 1919
1 July 1916
questions.explain: The Armistice came into effect at 11 a.m. on 11 November 1918, ending the fighting.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE History (0470) syllabus; Depth Study: The First World War 1914-18
